article.description: The UN’s top humanitarian official in Ukraine on Thursday condemned a Russian drone attack on the city of Dnipro that killed at least 13 civilians and injured
paragraphs: Firefighters work at the site of a Russian missile strike in Dnipro, Ukraine, Nov. 21, 2024. Photo Credit: Ukrainian Emergency Service
The UN’s top humanitarian official in Ukraine on Thursday condemned a Russian drone attack on the city of Dnipro that killed at least 13 civilians and injured 10 others at its main railway station.

“Civilians preparing for a trip, welcoming or bidding farewell to loved ones faced death and devastation,” said Matthias Schmale, the Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine, adding that displaced people and humanitarian workers at a transit centre at the station were left in shock by the nearby explosions.

Media outlets reported that a jet-powered drone hit the station as a train due to travel to Zaporizhzhia stood at a platform. An 11-year-old boy was among the injured, according to regional officials cited in the reports.
Mr. Schmale expressed condolences to the families of those killed on behalf of the UN, noting that train travel is a key means of transportation in Ukraine.

Photo: Wikipedia Explosions were heard near Iran’s Qeshm Island early Friday, October 30, as reports emerged of a US attack on an Iranian army naval base on the island.

Iranian news agency Urgent News reported preliminary information suggesting that US forces had targeted the naval installation, linking the explosions heard earlier to the attack. It did not provide details about the extent of the damage or possible casualties.

Separately, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim News Agency , citing unnamed sources, reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force intercepted a fighter jet described as “hostile” near Qeshm Island and forced it to leave the area.
The agency did not identify the aircraft or disclose its nationality. It also said no official statement had been issued confirming the interception.
Iran’s Fars News Agency reported that explosions were heard at sea near Qeshm Island and Sirik, in Hormozgan province, close to the Strait of Hormuz.

Join our Whatsapp channel Sanaa [Yemen], October 31 (ANI): Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group has strongly rejected accusations of deploying a drone towards the Medina region, following a declaration by the Saudi-led military coalition that an unmanned aircraft had been intercepted and destroyed above the area amid a widening regional conflict tied to the US-Israeli war. The Houthis dismissed the coalition's version of events, accusing Riyadh of fabricating claims of a hostile assault. This latest diplomatic and military friction unfolds against a backdrop of cross-border strikes hitting critical petroleum sites, military facilities and aviation hubs, exacerbating international anxiety over the spillover of hostilities. Medina holds supreme spiritual importance as the sanctuary of the Prophet's Mosque, standing as Islam's second-most sacred city after Mecca and drawing millions of faithful annually, particularly during the annual Haj and Umrah pilgrimages. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree denied that insurgent forces had carried out any military operation directed at Saudi territory. "The Yemeni Armed Forces affirm that they have not carried out any operation directed towards the Saudi interior. The claim by the criminal Saudi enemy that a drone was shot down in the airspace of Medina is merely a continuation of their grand and egregious fabrications," Saree said in a social media post. Prior to this statement, the Saudi-led military coalition announced that it had successfully intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by insurgent elements over the Medina governorate. These developments echo previous accusations by Riyadh alleging that the Houthis had attempted to target Mecca and Medina. The movement has consistently dismissed such claims, asserting that its military operations focus exclusively on infrastructure and defence installations, while pledging to transparently claim responsibility for operations carried out. In a previous escalation, national civil defence authorities reported that shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles had fallen across the Mecca and Medina territories, with scattered debris noted near Mecca, as well as Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. The Houthis rejected responsibility for targeting the holy sites on that occasion as well. The ongoing friction compounds a series of Houthi-claimed attacks targeting the Kingdom throughout the month, featuring strikes focused on major oil installations and airports. On October 3, the movement claimed credit for a missile and drone attack directed at an Aramco facility in Riyadh. A subsequent strike on October 13 sparked a major fire at Saudi Aramco's primary headquarters in Dhahran, followed by further claims targeting Aramco assets in Dhahran and a petroleum refinery in Riyadh on October 14. Civil aviation infrastructure has faced recurrent assaults. A Houthi-claimed attack directed at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10 resulted in 12 fatalities and 309 injuries, according to official Kingdom reports, while two preceding strikes earlier that week claimed four lives and damaged a commercial transport aircraft. In a separate incident last week, an assault on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam caused two deaths, comprising a Saudi national and an Indian citizen, alongside eight injuries. Furthermore, insurgent leadership has issued warnings cautioning commercial airlines against using Saudi airspace, while carving out specific exemptions for the skies above Mecca and Medina. This latest confrontation has severely fractured the fragile stability secured through a UN-sponsored truce in 2022, which had previously halted cross-border attacks between the alliance and the movement. While the coalition maintains support for Yemen's internationally recognised administration, the Houthis retain firm control over the capital, Sanaa, and extensive territories across northern Yemen. The renewed hostilities are unfolding in parallel with the ongoing US-Israeli war, as the Houthis escalate their operational tempo against Saudi assets. Geographical positioning grants the group direct leverage over vital maritime chokepoints. Stationed adjacent to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a foundational maritime corridor linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, the group poses acute vulnerabilities for global commercial navigation and energy transit lines. Riyadh has grown increasingly reliant on its domestic East-West pipeline network to route petroleum exports towards Red Sea terminals as regional disruptions restrict maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Mecca and Medina remain Islam's two most hallowed metropolitan centres, anchoring profound spiritual devotion across the global Muslim community. Mecca encompasses the revered Kaaba, serving as the directional focal point for daily prayers and the emotional epicentre of the annual Haj pilgrimage, while Medina houses the Prophet's Mosque, welcoming continuous streams of pilgrims year-round. The recurring cycle of official accusations and outright denials concerning strikes directed at these sacred cities adds an exceptionally sensitive dimension to the unfolding confrontation between Riyadh and the Houthis. article.title: India, Turkey proposing ideas for passage of grain shipments in Black Sea: Marco Rubio
article.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday stated India and Turkey have proposed ideas for vessels carrying grain to pass the Black Sea amid strikes in the wake of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. As Rubio hosted the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, speaking to the press, he said that passage of vessels through the Strait of Hormuz is even more challenging. He noted that the US has received limited cooperation in Hormuz despite President Donald Trump's call to join Washington's efforts in the region. Rubio said, "When you talk about the Black Sea, you saw a lot of countries speak up and express their willingness to contribute. Both Turkey and India have come to the table with some ideas about how we can get grain shipments moving because this is threatening global food security and, to some extent, energy security as well." "In the case of the Strait of Hormuz, it's more challenging, because many countries around the world don't have the ability to project power in the region. The President has repeatedly asked countries to join us in the effort to protect global shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. So far, we've had very limited cooperation, but not much. The responsibility has primarily fallen on the United States to protect shipping," he added. Further, he also took note of territorial claims on waterways in the Indo-Pacific region as a maritime challenge in the region. He said, "Obviously, in the Indo-Pacific, we don't have active kinetic operations taking place like those we're seeing in the Strait of Hormuz or even in the Black Sea. But we do face some challenges, including territorial claims that we do not recognise. That's why you see us not only maintaining a presence in that part of the world but also operating jointly and cooperatively with our partners to continue making it clear that we do not accept illegitimate territorial claims over waterways that are either international waters or not the territorial waters of any single nation." US and Iran have exchanged strikes amid a "blockade" in the strategic waterways of the Strait of Hormuz. While Iran continues to strike commercial vehicles, the United States reportedly struck two fishing boats off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, injuring two Iranian fishermen. As reported by the news agency IRNA, the two fishermen who went missing after the drone attack have been found, according to the CEO of the Qeshm Fishing Community. Both were sent back to Qeshm Island. Meanwhile, one of the two injured fishermen was taken to a hospital, Al Jazeera reported, citing Fars news agency. Meanwhile, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan noted that the situation in the Black Sea is on the agenda for the meeting between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Even the Quad Foreign Ministers on Saturday called for preserving navigational rights and freedoms in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait against the backdrop of tensions in West Asia.
